title: How to Start a Sermon: The First Ninety Seconds
subtitle: How to begin a sermon with an introduction that earns attention, opens the text, and never cheapens it, with practical patterns for the first ninety seconds in the pulpit.

sections.title: Why the First Ninety Seconds Decide Everything
sections.body:
The sermon is won or lost before you reach your first point.

A congregation makes a decision in the opening seconds, and they make it below the level of thought. They decide whether this man has anything to say. They decide whether to lean in or drift off toward the lunch they are already planning. You will not get that decision back. A weak introduction does not merely waste ninety seconds. It teaches the room that today is a day to coast, and the rest of your work pays the price.

Most of us know this and respond with the wrong fix. We reach for the joke, the clip, the startling statistic, the story that has nothing to do with the text but everything to do with getting a laugh. We win the room and lose the sermon, because we trained them to expect entertainment and then asked them to receive a word from God. The introduction is not a warmup act. It is the door you open into the text, and the kind of door you build tells them what kind of house they are entering.

sections.title: Raise the Question the Text Answers
sections.body:
A good introduction does one thing. It creates the need the passage will meet.

Every text in Scripture answers a question, scratches an itch, names a wound. Your job in the opening is to make the people feel that question as their own before you ever read the verse. Not to summarize what you will say. To open a gap. To raise a tension they did not know they were carrying until you named it, and then to promise, by your manner more than your words, that the text in front of them speaks to exactly that.

So do not begin with the answer. Begin with the ache. If the passage is about anxiety, do not announce that you are preaching on anxiety. Describe the three in the morning waking, the running ledger of everything that could go wrong, the prayer that feels like talking to the ceiling. Make them feel found before you offer to lead them anywhere. Then the text arrives not as an assignment but as relief, because you spent your first minute making them want it.

sections.title: Four Openings That Earn the Right
sections.body:
You do not need a new idea every week. You need a few honest doors and the wisdom to choose.

The concrete scene. Drop them into a moment, plainly told, that embodies the tension of the text. The hospital hallway. The unread text message. The empty chair at the table. No commentary. Let the picture do the work and trust them to feel it.

The honest confession. Begin inside yourself. Name the place where this text exposes you before it exposes them. A preacher who says I have failed at exactly this has bought himself an enormous amount of trust in eleven words.

The hard question. Ask the thing the room is afraid to ask out loud. Why does God let this go on. Is forgiveness even possible after that. Then sit in it long enough that they know you are not going to dodge.

The arresting verse. Sometimes the text itself is the best opening. Read it cold, let the strangeness land, and ask what kind of God says a thing like this. The trick in all four is restraint. You are opening a door, not redecorating the room.

sections.title: The Openings That Sabotage You
sections.body:
Most bad introductions share the same flaw. They are about the preacher, not the people.

The apology kills the room. Do not tell them you are tired, underprepared, or unsure how this one came together. They came for a word from God and you just told them not to expect one. The throat clearing does the same damage more slowly. Good morning, so glad you are here, before we get started I want to mention three announcements, now where was I. You have spent your most valuable thirty seconds on logistics and your sermon never recovers its altitude.

The unrelated story is the most seductive trap. It is funny. It works. And it has nothing to do with the text, so when you pivot, the room feels the seam, and they learn that the opening and the sermon are two different products. Preach the warmup or cut it.

And beware the long runway. If your introduction is five minutes, it is not an introduction. It is a separate sermon you have to abandon to start the real one. Ninety seconds. Two minutes if the room is heavy. Then the text. Get in, raise the need, and get out of the way.

sections.title: Handing the Room to the Text
sections.body:
The introduction has one job left. To deliver the room to the passage and disappear.

The handoff is the most neglected sentence in most sermons. You raised the ache, you opened the door, and now you have to walk them across the threshold without breaking the spell. This is not the place for here is what I want to do today. It is the place for a single sentence that takes the tension you built and lays it directly on the text. The question we have been circling, the text in front of us answers it without flinching. Then read the verse.

When the handoff works, the people do not notice they have moved from your words to God's. The need you created flows straight into the passage and the passage takes over. That is the whole aim. Your introduction was never the point. It was the welcome at the door of a house you did not build.

The best preachers are almost invisible in their first two minutes. They create hunger, point to the table, and step back. Learn that and you will never lose a room in the first ninety seconds again. Lose it there, and no amount of brilliance in the body will get it back.
